summary: Describes the Lightweight Access Point Protocol, a proposal for centralized control of wireless access points by an Access Controller, moving functions like authentication, mobility and radio management out of the access points. It was submitted as input to the CAPWAP working group. This is a historic document.

eli5.summary: Instead of every wifi box making its own decisions, one boss computer decides for all of them. This describes one early plan for how the boss talks to the boxes.

questions: how does a wireless controller manage access points
subtitle: An early way for a central controller to manage many wireless access points

tldr.problem: Wireless access points (WiFi boxes) traditionally work independently, making decisions about user authentication, security, and radio settings on their own. This makes networks hard to manage at scale. Network operators wanted a way for one central controller to manage all the access points.
tldr.mechanism: LWAPP defines how lightweight access points (WTPs) communicate with a central Access Controller (AC). The AC controls authentication, security policies, and radio management, while the WTPs handle just the wireless transmission. WTPs discover an AC, join it, receive configuration, and forward wireless frames through the LWAPP protocol.
tldr.outcome: LWAPP was submitted to the CAPWAP working group as input. RFC 5415 later defined the standards-track CAPWAP protocol, which superseded LWAPP. RFC 5412 is now Historic and documents the original proposal.

facts.value: Idle, Discovery, Sulking, Join, Join-Confirm, Configure, Run, Key Update, Image Data, Reset

facts.label: Control message encryption
facts.value: AES or 3DES with derived session keys

today: RFC 5412 is Historic. The standards-track solution for wireless access point control is RFC 5415 (CAPWAP - Control and Provisioning of Wireless Access Points). RFC 5412 is published for historical record only; new implementations must use RFC 5415.

sections.title: Centralized Wireless Control
sections.content:
LWAPP (Lightweight Access Point Protocol) defines how a centralized Access Controller (AC) manages a collection of Wireless Termination Points (WTPs). Traditional access points are autonomous: each one handles user authentication, security, mobility, and radio management independently. This approach becomes unmanageable in large networks.

LWAPP moves these functions from the access points to a central controller. The WTPs become lightweight devices that handle only wireless transmission and reception, forwarding all management decisions to the AC. The AC can enforce consistent security policies, manage user roaming, and configure radios remotely across many WTPs. LWAPP is designed to be technology-independent, with specific bindings for wireless protocols like IEEE 802.11 (WiFi).
sections.eli5: Instead of every WiFi box making its own decisions about who can connect and what to do, one central boss computer makes all those decisions and tells each box what to do.

sections.title: Protocol Architecture and State Machine
sections.content:
LWAPP defines two transport options: Layer 2 (direct Ethernet) or Layer 3 (IP/UDP). Both WTPs and the AC run a state machine with states like Idle, Discovery, Join, Configure, Run, and Key Update. The protocol begins with discovery: WTPs send Discovery Requests and ACs respond. The WTP selects the best AC and sends a Join Request, which triggers mutual authentication and key establishment. During the Configure state, the WTP and AC exchange configuration information, including WiFi settings like SSID and security parameters. Finally, the WTP enters the Run state to forward wireless frames and statistics.

The protocol supports keepalive via Echo messages to detect AC failures, triggering rediscovery. It also defines a Sulking state where a WTP waits before retrying discovery after multiple failures.
sections.eli5: The access point and controller go through steps: first find each other (discovery), then shake hands to agree on security (join), then the AC tells the AP its WiFi settings (configure), then the AP is ready to handle WiFi traffic (run). If the controller stops responding, the AP notices and looks for a new controller.

sections.title: Message Types and Protocol Operations
sections.content:
LWAPP uses two message types: data messages (forwarded wireless frames) and control messages (protocol management). Control messages include: Discovery (find an AC), Join (connect to an AC), Configure (exchange settings), Echo (keepalive), Key Update (refresh encryption keys), WTP Event (send statistics and events), and Mobile Config (manage connected devices).

Each message uses a base LWAPP header with fields like Version, Radio ID, Control/Data bit, Fragment ID, and Length. Messages can be fragmented if they exceed the maximum transmission unit. For 802.11, message elements also include wireless-specific parameters such as SSID, transmit power, channel information, and supported rates.
sections.eli5: The protocol has messages for 'hello, are you there?', 'I want to join you', 'here are my settings', 'I am alive', 'let's refresh the secret encryption key', and 'here are the WiFi devices connected to me'.

sections.title: Security and Encryption
sections.content:
LWAPP control messages are encrypted to protect against unauthorized access. The protocol supports two key establishment methods: certificate-based (using X.509 certificates) and pre-shared key (PSK). After initial authentication, the WTP and AC derive session keys using nonces (random values): the WTP provides an XNonce, the AC provides an ANonce, and the WTP provides a WNonce. These are combined to generate encryption keys.

The protocol includes a Key Update Request mechanism that allows periodic rekeying, where new encryption keys are derived and installed without interrupting service. Control message authenticity is verified using HMAC-based Message Integrity Checks (PSK-MIC). All LWAPP control frames are encrypted using the session key and an initialization vector.
sections.eli5: The access point and controller prove they trust each other using either certificates (like a passport) or a shared secret password. Then they work together to create an encryption key that protects all their secret messages. They can refresh this key regularly without stopping.

sections.title: IEEE 802.11 Binding and Historical Status
sections.content:
LWAPP can be adapted for different wireless technologies through bindings. The RFC includes a comprehensive binding for IEEE 802.11 (WiFi) that defines how to map 802.11 concepts (like SSIDs, BSSID, security modes, and transmission power) to LWAPP messages. The binding specifies two modes: Split MAC, where the AC handles MAC sublayer functions, and Local MAC, where the WTP handles some MAC functions locally.

RFC 5412 is Historic. It documents LWAPP as submitted to the CAPWAP (Control and Provisioning of Wireless Access Points) working group. RFC 5415 defines the standards-track CAPWAP protocol, which refined and improved upon the LWAPP design. RFC 5415 should be used for any new implementations. LWAPP served as historical input to show how centralized wireless control could work.
sections.eli5: This RFC shows how to use the protocol with WiFi specifically. But this whole approach was just a proposal. The real standard that came later is called CAPWAP (RFC 5415), and that is what people use now.
